answer.reason: When identity verification must precede financial operations, compliance has to be deterministic. A programmatic prerequisite gate that blocks lookup_order and process_refund until get_customer returns a verified ID guarantees the order. Prompt instructions (B) and few-shot examples (C) still fail some of the time, and a routing classifier (D) does not enforce the order of tool calls.

Tool descriptions are the primary mechanism the model uses to choose between tools. Both descriptions here are minimal and overlap, so the low-effort, high-impact first step is to expand them: say what inputs each handles, give example queries, cover edge cases, and state when to use each tool over the other. Few-shot examples (A) add token cost without fixing the root cause. A keyword router (C) is over-engineered and bypasses the model's reasoning. Consolidating the tools (D) is a bigger architectural change than a first step warrants.

The root cause is unclear decision boundaries. Explicit escalation criteria plus few-shot examples (5.2-S1) directly fix this by showing when to resolve and when to escalate. Self-reported confidence and sentiment are unreliable proxies for case complexity (5.2-K3). A trained classifier is over-engineered as a first step.

Project-scoped commands go in .claude/commands/ inside the repository. Because that directory is under version control, every developer gets the /review command when they clone or pull. ~/.claude/commands/ is personal to each user and not shared. CLAUDE.md and config.json are not where slash commands are defined.

Microservice restructuring spans dozens of files and requires architectural decisions about service boundaries and dependencies. That is exactly what plan mode is for: exploring the codebase and designing an approach before committing to changes, which prevents costly rework.

Path-scoped rule files in .claude/rules/ use glob patterns in YAML frontmatter (e.g., **/*.test.tsx), so each convention loads automatically when Claude edits matching files, wherever they sit. Subdirectory CLAUDE.md files can't cover test files scattered across directories. Skills need manual invocation. A monolithic CLAUDE.md relies on Claude inferring which section applies.

The coordinator's logs show it split the topic into three visual-arts-only subtasks. The subagents then did exactly what they were assigned, so the coverage gap comes from the overly narrow decomposition (1.2-K4).

Structured error context (failure type, attempted query, partial results, alternatives) gives the coordinator what it needs to recover intelligently. The other options are anti-patterns: B returns a generic status that hides useful context, C silently suppresses the error, and D terminates the whole workflow over a single failure.

Per 2.3-S3, the synthesis agent gets a scoped cross-role tool such as verify_fact for the high-frequency simple fact-checks (85% of cases). Complex verifications still route through the coordinator, which keeps specialization intact and preserves observability. Option C gives synthesis too many tools and invites misuse. Option B still requires round trips and creates dependencies between checks. Option D relies on speculative caching that may not match what synthesis actually needs to verify.

The -p (--print) flag runs Claude Code in non-interactive mode: it processes the prompt, prints the result and exits, so the CI job won't hang. CLAUDE_HEADLESS and --batch are not real options, and redirecting stdin from /dev/null doesn't properly switch Claude Code to non-interactive mode.

The Batches API has no latency guarantee and can take up to 24 hours, so it doesn't fit a blocking pre-merge check. The overnight technical debt report tolerates that delay and can take the 50% savings.

Per-file local passes plus a separate cross-file integration pass avoid the attention dilution and contradictory findings of a single pass, while still catching issues that span files (1.6-S2, 4.6-S2).
